name: Ethiopian

database_scope.purpose: Sourced reference for Ethiopian minhagim and halachic practice. It records what the cited sources say, with a confidence level for each entry, and is not a psak.
database_scope.coverage_note: 35 sourced topics and 6 distinctive customs, compiled from the cited sources in October 2026. Each entry carries a confidence level (well-attested, disputed, regional, needs-review). 15 topics have no community-specific source and are listed under 'gaps' rather than filled with generic text.

identity.primary_origin: Northern Ethiopia: the Gondar region (Dembia), Tigray, Semien and Quara
secondary_centers: Israel (since Operation Moses in 1984 and Operation Solomon in 1991)

languages: Ge'ez: the language of the Orit and of the community's liturgical books
Amharic and Tigrinya: the languages the prayers and readings are translated into; Tigrinya is spoken by the Tigrean communities

subgroups.name: Gondar / Dembia
subgroups.note: The largest population and the source of most documented practice. Kaplan (Encyclopaedia Judaica) notes it benefited more from world-Jewry education efforts than Tigray did. Most came via Sudan from 1984 or in Operation Solomon (1991).

subgroups.name: Tigray / Walqayit
subgroups.note: Encyclopaedia Judaica (Kaplan): the modern Tigrean communities 'appear to have originated in 1862'. They speak Tigrinya and had 'no common leadership' with Gondar. Most pre-1984 immigrants came from Tigre and Walqayit. A 'latent hostility' with Gondar carried over into Israel. No ritual differences are documented.

subgroups.name: Semien (Simien)
subgroups.note: Seat of the last Beta Israel autonomous rule, ended in 1626 (Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center). No distinct ritual is documented.

subgroups.name: Quara (Qwara)
subgroups.note: Emigration was blocked by rebel control and took place 1992–1999, about 5,000 people (Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center). The liturgy contains Agaw passages (Shelemay 1986), but no source links them to Qwara.

subgroups.name: Kessim and monks (kahenat/qesoch, maloksewoch)
subgroups.note: Leadership tradition that holds the Orit and the oral tradition.

subgroups.name: Falash Mura / Zera Beta Israel
subgroups.note: Descendants of Beta Israel who converted to Christianity from the 19th century. About 50,000 have come to Israel in waves, and conversion is required (Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center).

subgroups.name: Ethiopian Israelis
subgroups.note: About 177,600 people in 2024, about 2.3% of Israel's Jewish population, per Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics (Sigd 2025 release, reported by JNS). The Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center splits this as 93,400 Ethiopia-born and 84,200 Israel-born. Practice ranges from Orit/kessim tradition to Shulchan Aruch, often mixed.

timeline.event: Emperor Yeshaq: those not baptised lose their land and become 'Felase' (landless).
timeline.halachic_impact: Possible origin of 'Falasha' and background to later conversions (Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center).

timeline.event: Abba Sabra and Saga Amlak lead a revival. Prayers and purity laws are attributed to them.
timeline.halachic_impact: Source of the strict purity boundaries (Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center).

timeline.event: R. Elijah of Ferrara reports they have 'the Torah and an oral commentary', 'neither the Talmud nor our poskim', and Esther but not Chanukah. The Radbaz rules they are of the tribe of Dan.
timeline.halachic_impact: Precedent for R. Ovadia Yosef (Avi Harel).

timeline.event: Abba Mahari's march toward Jerusalem. Survivors settle in Tigray.
timeline.halachic_impact: Origin of the Tigray/Gondar split (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

timeline.event: Faitlovitch introduces Sabbath candles and post-biblical holidays, and discourages sacrifice and the seclusion of menstruating women.
R. Kook and R. Yaakov Meir call to save the 'Falashas'.
R. Herzog requires giyur lechumra (precautionary conversion): immersion plus hatafat dam brit (a symbolic drop of blood from the circumcision site).
timeline.halachic_impact: Start of the precautionary-conversion requirement (Moav, Deot 86). Upheld by the Supreme Court for marriage in 1966 (Harel).

timeline.event: R. Ovadia Yosef: 'הפלאשים הם יהודים שחייבים להצילם מטמיעה ומהתבוללות ולהחיש עלייתם ארצה… ולחנכם ברוח תורתנו' ('The Falashas are Jews whom we must save from assimilation, hasten their aliyah… and educate in the spirit of our Torah').

R. Goren recognises them. An inter-ministerial team rules them Jews for the Law of Return (April 1975, per Harel), and the Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center states that the State 'accepted Rabbi Ovadia's ruling and on July 25, 1975, included Ethiopian Jewry under the Law of Return.'
timeline.halachic_impact: Aliyah eligibility. Conversion was still demanded for marriage.

timeline.event: Chief Rabbinate Council: 'בחזקת יהודים' (presumed Jews), but conversion by circumcision, immersion and acceptance of mitzvot 'due to concern of intermixture'.

Operation Moses: more than 6,000 people according to the Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center, while the World Jewish Congress (2020) says it began on 18 November 1984 and brought 'approximately 8,000 Ethiopian Jews… aboard 30 flights'.
timeline.halachic_impact: Mass arrival brings the conversion question to a head.

timeline.event: The Council drops hatafat dam but keeps immersion and a halachic undertaking. Goren and Yosef publicly disagree. A month-long protest at Hechal Shlomo begins 5 September. The Rabbinate then confines doubt to individual marriage cases.
timeline.halachic_impact: Extra scrutiny of individual marriage files (JTA 1985; Moav).

timeline.event: Operation Solomon: 14,325 Ethiopian Jews flown nonstop on 35 Israeli aircraft (IAF C-130s and El Al 747s) 'to safety in Israel in 36 hours' (Israel Hayom, 25 May 2021).
timeline.halachic_impact: Almost the whole community now under Israeli religious jurisdiction.

timeline.event: Tzaban Commission (September 1992): Falash Mura are not Jews under the Law of Return. In 2002 R. Amar, with R. Ovadia, rules them of Jewish descent and to be returned to Judaism.
timeline.halachic_impact: Falash Mura conversion or return after arrival.

timeline.event: The Knesset passes the Sigd Law.
The State recognises kessim as spiritual leaders, with 20 funded posts and no authority over weddings.
The Chief Rabbinate Council re-adopts R. Ovadia's ruling. R. Yehuda Deri: 'קהילת יהודי אתיופיה הם יהודים כשרים לכל דבר' ('The Ethiopian Jewish community are Jews, fully kosher in every respect').
timeline.halachic_impact: Ends the formal basis for special checks. Does not apply to Falash Mura.

timeline.event: Operation Tzur Israel: the first phase brought 2,000 people on 9 flights between December 2020 and 11 March 2021, per the Jewish Agency. A late-2021 government decision approved 3,000 new immigrants in total (Times of Israel, June 2022). eJewishPhilanthropy (July 2023) reports about 5,000 arrivals across two phases. Times of Israel estimates about 40,000 have come under the Law of Entry since 1992.

primary_codes: Orit: the Ge'ez Octateuch (the Five Books of Moses plus Joshua, Judges and Ruth), handwritten on parchment as a bound book
Liturgical books: Mäṣḥafä Sa'atat (Book of Hours); 'Sefer Cahen' (NACOEJ)
Other Ge'ez works: Enoch, Jubilees, Baruch, Ezra books, Gadla Avraham/Yitzhak/Ya'akov
major_rishonim_base: Not part of traditional Beta Israel practice, which had no Talmud
For Israeli status rulings: Radbaz (מארץ כוש הם משבט דן בלי ספק, 'those from Kush are of the tribe of Dan without doubt'; tinok shenishba, a Jew raised without knowledge of the law) and Maharikash
later_poskim: R. Avraham Shapira and R. Mordechai Eliyahu (1984–85)
Community rabbis R. Yosef Hadane and R. Sharon Shalom
core_halachic_authorities.decision_principle: Traditional law is the written Torah as found in the Ge'ez Orit, interpreted through the kessim's and monks' oral tradition. NACOEJ: 'the Written Law and oral interpretations… passed down from generation to generation, of the community's own holy writings'. There was no Talmud. Authority was local: each village followed its kes and elders, under a regional liqa kahenat (chief priest). In Israel, the Chief Rabbinate applies Shulchan Aruch-based halacha to personal status, marriage, conversion and kashrut, and does not treat kessim as rabbis. Since 2018 the State recognises kessim as 'spiritual leaders' with limited, non-marital functions.

runtime.practice_baseline: Traditional practice rests on the Ge'ez Orit and kessim oral tradition, not the Talmud or Shulchan Aruch; in Israel personal status is governed by Chief Rabbinate application of Shulchan Aruch-based halacha.

parameters.source: Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center, 'The Sigd Holiday' (Sigd Law 2008)

parameters.value: If 29 Cheshvan is Shabbat, observe on Thursday 27 Cheshvan
parameters.source: Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center, 'The Sigd Holiday'

parameters.value: 12th of the third month; 50 days counted from the day after the end of Pesach

halacha_index.summary: The holiest text is the Orit: the Ge'ez Octateuch, handwritten on parchment as a bound book. The Prophets and Writings are secondary. Enoch, Jubilees, Baruch and the Ezra books are also sacred.
common_practices: The Orit is kept in the mesgid's inner sanctum (kadesta kedusan) or in a kes's home
Since 2016 the National Library of Israel holds a digitised Orit, and a 2024 project with Tel Aviv University's 'Orit Guardians' programme is digitising more manuscripts
halacha_index.source: NACOEJ, 'Religious Practices of Ethiopian Jews', pp. 2–3; Times of Israel, NLI digitization report (Oct. 2024)
halacha_index.review_notes: No firm line between canonical and non-canonical texts.
halacha_index.summary_he: הטקסט הקדוש ביותר הוא האורית: שמונת הספרים הראשונים בגעז, כתובים ביד על קלף בצורת ספר כרוך. הנביאים והכתובים משניים. גם חנוך, היובלים, ברוך וספרי עזרא קדושים.

halacha_index.summary: Kessim led prayer, offered sacrifices, ruled on purity, marriage and divorce, taught, mediated disputes, imposed sanctions and accepted converts. Monks (maloksewoch) trained and ordained them. Each region had a liqa kahenat (chief priest).
common_practices: Training from about age 7–8
Ordained only after marriage and with the community's approval
A kes marries only a virgin
Kessim wear white turbans and garments
Supported by first fruits and donations
Not hereditary descendants of Aaron (NACOEJ)

variants.practice: Kessim took over ordination
variants.source: Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center, 'About Ethiopian Jewry'

halacha_index.source: Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center, 'About Ethiopian Jewry'; NACOEJ, 'Religious Practices', p. 1
halacha_index.review_notes: Encyclopaedia Judaica (Kaplan): no centralised institutions; 'Chaque commune est autonomie et indépendante' ('each commune is autonomous and independent', Halévy).

halacha_index.summary_he: הקייסים הובילו את התפילה, הקריבו קורבנות, פסקו בענייני טהרה, נישואין וגירושין, לימדו, גישרו בסכסוכים, הטילו סנקציות וקיבלו גרים. נזירים (מלוקסוצ'ים) הכשירו והסמיכו אותם. בכל אזור היה ליקה כהנת (כהן גדול).

halacha_index.summary: The Chief Rabbinate does not recognise kessim as rabbis because they were not trained in the Oral Law. On 19 February 2018 the Ministerial Committee chaired by PM Netanyahu recognised them as 'spiritual leaders'. November 2018 recommendations allow kessim to conduct holiday ceremonies, the pre-burial part of funerals, and mourning and purification rites, but not weddings. Twenty funded positions were created.
common_practices: Appointment panel: the local religious council, the local kes and a Ministry-appointed kes
Ethiopian-origin rabbis are to sit on religious councils
halacha_index.source: Al-Monitor, D. Zaken (2 Mar. 2018); Haaretz (8 Nov. 2018); JTA archive on the kessim protests
halacha_index.review_notes: Earlier, Rabbinate-ordained Ethiopian rabbis could serve only Ethiopian communities. How far the 2018 framework has been implemented by 2026 is unverified.

halacha_index.summary_he: הרבנות הראשית אינה מכירה בקייסים כרבנים, מפני שלא הוכשרו בתורה שבעל פה. ב-19 בפברואר 2018 ועדת השרים בראשות ראש הממשלה נתניהו הכירה בהם כ"מנהיגים רוחניים". המלצות נובמבר 2018 מתירות לקייסים לערוך טקסי חג, את החלק שלפני הקבורה בלוויה, וטקסי אבל וטהרה, אך לא חתונות. נוצרו עשרים תקנים ממומנים.

halacha_index.summary: Ruling of 7 Adar I 5733: the 'Falashas' are Jews whom Israel must save from assimilation, bring on aliyah and educate in the Torah. It relies on the Radbaz, Maharikash, R. Hildesheimer, R. Kook and R. Herzog. The April 1975 inter-ministerial finding under the Law of Return rests on it, and the Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center dates the State's formal inclusion of Ethiopian Jewry under the Law of Return to 25 July 1975.
halacha_index.source: Avi Harel (2015), quoting the ruling; Ethiopian Jewry Heritage Center
halacha_index.review_notes: The Yabia Omer text was not opened. Sources disagree on whether he required symbolic conversion at first (see disputes).

halacha_index.summary_he: פסק מז' באדר א' תשל"ג: ה"פלשים" הם יהודים שישראל חייבת להצילם מהתבוללות, להעלותם ולחנכם בתורה. הוא נשען על הרדב"ז, המהרי"קש, רבי הילדסהיימר, הרב קוק והרב הרצוג. הקביעה הבין-משרדית מאפריל 1975 לפי חוק השבות נשענת עליו, ומרכז המורשת של יהדות אתיופיה מתארך את הכללתה הרשמית של יהדות אתיופיה בחוק השבות ל-25 ביולי 1975.

halacha_index.summary: R. Goren initially held back, then recognised them: 'You are our brothers, you are our blood and our flesh. You are true Jews.' In 1985 he said neither immersion nor symbolic circumcision was required. Sources date his first recognition to 1974 or 1975, and he and R. Ovadia Yosef publicly disagreed in 1985.

variants.practice: Recognised them as Jews. In 1985 he said neither immersion nor symbolic circumcision was required.

variants.subgroup: Chief Rabbinate Council (5 Nov. 1984; revised early 1985)
variants.practice: Presumed them Jews but required immersion and an undertaking to observe halacha, out of concern for intermixture.

halacha_index.review_notes: Dated 1974 or 1975 depending on the source. Primary letter not found.

halacha_index.summary_he: הרב גורן הסס בתחילה ואחר כך הכיר בהם: "אתם אחינו, אתם דמנו ובשרנו. אתם יהודים אמיתיים". ב-1985 אמר שאין צורך לא בטבילה ולא בהטפת דם ברית. המקורות מתארכים את הכרתו הראשונה ל-1974 או ל-1975, והוא והרב עובדיה יוסף נחלקו בפומבי ב-1985.

halacha_index.summary: R. Herzog (1954) required immersion and hatafat dam. The Council (5 November 1984) required circumcision, immersion and acceptance of mitzvot. In early 1985 the Council under R. Shapira and R. Eliyahu dropped hatafat dam (the men were already circumcised) but kept immersion and an undertaking to observe halacha.
common_practices: Immersion before three rabbis, without a blessing (Moav)
Marriage certificates refused to those who had not immersed

variants.practice: Reportedly, immersion before marriage only in cases of doubt
variants.source: Kulanu, 'Return of a Lost Tribe' (an advocacy organization)

halacha_index.review_notes: Hechal Shlomo protest from 5 September 1985 (Ono Academic College). See Kaplan, Social Science Information 27:3 (1988).

halacha_index.summary_he: הרב הרצוג (1954) דרש טבילה והטפת דם. מועצת הרבנות (5 בנובמבר 1984) דרשה מילה, טבילה וקבלת מצוות. בתחילת 1985 המועצה בראשות הרב שפירא והרב אליהו ביטלה את הטפת הדם (הגברים כבר היו מולים) אך השאירה את הטבילה ואת ההתחייבות לשמור הלכה.

halacha_index.summary: In November 2019 the Chief Rabbinate Council adopted R. Ovadia's ruling. Kan reported it on 19 January 2020. R. Yehuda Deri: they are fully kosher Jews, to be checked only as all communities are. Excludes the Falash Mura.
halacha_index.source: JTA, M. Oster (21 Jan. 2020); Haaretz (Hebrew), 19 Jan. 2020
halacha_index.review_notes: R. Sharon Shalom called it 'too little too late' and said no official document had been seen.

halacha_index.summary_he: בנובמבר 2019 אימצה מועצת הרבנות הראשית את פסק הרב עובדיה. תאגיד "כאן" דיווח על כך ב-19 בינואר 2020. הרב יהודה דרעי: הם יהודים כשרים לגמרי, ויש לבדוק אותם רק כפי שבודקים את כל העדות. הדבר אינו כולל את הפלשמורה.

halacha_index.summary: Repeated extra scrutiny, notably in Petah Tikva. The Rabbinate arranged for 14 Ethiopian-community rabbis to register and perform marriages. An October 2013 law allows couples to register anywhere in the country.
common_practices: Tzohar asks Ethiopian immigrants for 'confirmation of your Jewish identity from an authorised rabbi from your community'
Kessim cannot officiate legally recognised weddings
halacha_index.source: Times of Israel (Petah Tikva report); Tzohar 'Marriage Registration' guide
halacha_index.review_notes: R. Yosef Hadane was forced to retire in 2016, reportedly over his criticism. Current procedure is unverified.

halacha_index.summary_he: בדיקה חוזרת ומוגברת, בעיקר בפתח תקווה. הרבנות סידרה ש-14 רבנים מהעדה האתיופית ירשמו וייערכו נישואין. חוק מאוקטובר 2013 מאפשר לזוגות להירשם בכל מקום בארץ.

halacha_index.summary: The Tzaban Commission (1992) found them not Jews under the Law of Return. R. Amar (2002), seconded by R. Ovadia, ruled those of maternal Jewish descent must be brought and returned to Judaism. They enter only by government decision, conditional on Orthodox conversion. Some within the Beta Israel community deny maternal Jewish descent for recent applicants.

Pre-aliyah study, tallit and tefillin in Gondar under R. Menachem Waldman
At least 11 government resolutions since 1992

Not Jews under the Law of Return.

halacha_index.summary_he: ועדת צבן (1992) קבעה שהם אינם יהודים לפי חוק השבות. הרב עמאר (2002), בהסכמת הרב עובדיה, פסק שמי שיש לו מוצא יהודי מצד האם יש להביאו ולהחזירו ליהדות. הם נכנסים רק בהחלטת ממשלה, בתנאי גיור אורתודוקסי. יש בתוך קהילת בית ישראל מי שמכחישים מוצא יהודי מצד האם אצל המבקשים האחרונים.

halacha_index.summary: Prayer in the mesgid is in Ge'ez. The congregation answers 'Amen' and sings known passages. Three weekday services: dawn, midday and dusk. Shabbat and festivals add services attended by the whole community.
common_practices: Prayer faces Jerusalem
Prostration, dance, drums and cymbals
Shoes removed
Only priests cover their heads
Women sit separately
Blessings open 'Itbarek Egzi'abeher Amlak Israel… Amlak of all flesh and all spirit'

variants.practice: Seven times daily until the last monk in the Ambober area died in the late 1960s

halacha_index.source: NACOEJ, 'Religious Practices', p. 3; Shelemay, 'Jewish Liturgical Forms in the Falasha Liturgy?' (1986)
halacha_index.review_notes: The liturgy includes Agaw passages (Shelemay).
halacha_index.summary_he: התפילה במסגיד היא בגעז. הקהל עונה "אמן" ושר קטעים מוכרים. שלוש תפילות בימי חול: עלות השחר, צהריים ובין הערביים. בשבת ובחגים נוספות תפילות שכל הקהילה משתתפת בהן.

halacha_index.summary: Preparation begins on Thursday and work stops at midday Friday. Women cook only after immersing. Stoves are put out before sunset and the embers doused. Food is eaten cold unless it was buried while warm. A light lit only for illumination may burn on Friday night until it goes out.
common_practices: A Shabbat-only candle
A robe with no belt, so no knots are tied
No leaving the village
Self-defence permitted

variants.practice: Rabbinic candle lighting introduced

halacha_index.source: NACOEJ, 'Religious Practices', pp. 2, 4–5 (with a Te'ezaza Sanbat translation)
halacha_index.review_notes: Single source. No Kabbalat Shabbat or Havdalah rite is documented.
halacha_index.summary_he: ההכנה מתחילה ביום חמישי והעבודה פוסקת בצהרי יום שישי. נשים מבשלות רק אחרי טבילה. מכבים את התנורים לפני השקיעה ומכבים את הגחלים. אוכלים אוכל קר, אלא אם נקבר כשהוא חם. אור שהודלק רק לצורך תאורה רשאי לדלוק בליל שבת עד שיכבה.

halacha_index.summary: After morning prayers each woman's maswaet ('gift offering') or baraketeh ('blessing') loaf is brought to the mesgid. The kahenat bless it and cut it in a special way, and it is eaten with a beer-like drink at a communal feast.
common_practices: Greeting 'Sanbat salam'
Second meal later in the day
Orit read in the local language, then a sermon
halacha_index.review_notes: No separate Kiddush over wine is documented.
halacha_index.summary_he: אחרי תפילת הבוקר מביאה כל אישה את לחם המסואט שלה ("מנחה") או הברכתה ("ברכה") למסגיד. הכהנת מברכות עליו וחותכות אותו בדרך מיוחדת, והוא נאכל עם משקה דמוי בירה בסעודה משותפת.

halacha_index.summary: Sabbaths run in cycles of seven, each with its own sunset prayer. The seventh is the holiest, with a special sanctification service.

halacha_index.summary_he: השבתות מתנהלות במחזורי שבע, ולכל אחת תפילת שקיעה משלה. השביעית היא הקדושה ביותר, עם תפילת קידוש מיוחדת.

halacha_index.summary: On 14 Nisan the paschal sacrifice is offered on a stone altar, roasted, and eaten on the eve of the 15th without breaking bones. For seven days there is no leaven. Dishes are replaced, and the five grains, 'certain forms of legume', fermented foods and non-fresh milk products are avoided. A special matzah, kitta, is baked. The kahenat tell the Exodus story orally.

halacha_index.summary: Work stops on every new moon. The 10th, 12th and 15th of each month recall Yom Kippur, Shavuot, and Pesach/Sukkot. 1 Nisan is the Festival of Lissan. The 12th of the ninth month is a harvest festival. The 18th of the sixth month commemorates the patriarchs.

halacha_index.summary_he: העבודה פוסקת בכל ראש חודש. העשירי, השנים עשר והחמישה עשר בכל חודש מזכירים את יום כיפור, שבועות, ופסח וסוכות. א' בניסן הוא חג הליסאן. י"ב בחודש התשיעי הוא חג קציר. י"ח בחודש השישי מציין את האבות.

halacha_index.summary: The community's own lunar calendar. The rabbinic leap rules and the year count since creation were unknown, but festival dates are 'very close' to those of other Jews. Months: Lissan, Tomas, Ab, Lul, Tahasrein, Tabt. Months are counted from Nisan.

In the afternoon they descend and break the fast with sacrificial beef and dancing.

halacha_index.summary: The kes slaughters facing Jerusalem, after a blessing that includes the Ten Commandments. The blood is covered, the meat cut small, soaked, washed and dried, and always cooked. The sciatic nerve and certain fats are removed. Meat and milk are not cooked together. Poultry is not counted as meat. Food touched by gentiles is forbidden.
halacha_index.review_notes: In Israel the Rabbinate standard applies (see disputes on the Barkan winery case).
halacha_index.summary_he: הקייס שוחט בפנים לירושלים, אחרי ברכה הכוללת את עשרת הדיברות. מכסים את הדם, חותכים את הבשר לחתיכות קטנות, משרים, שוטפים ומייבשים, ותמיד מבשלים אותו. מסירים את גיד הנשה ואת חלבים מסוימים. אין מבשלים בשר וחלב יחד. עוף אינו נחשב בשר. אוכל שנגעו בו גויים אסור.

halacha_index.summary: Villages are built near water. Corpse impurity is removed with mai manzeh ('water of sprinkling', made with red heifer ash), applied on days 3 and 7, followed by immersion, with seven days spent outside the village. Non-Jews are treated as impure.
halacha_index.review_notes: Also reported by the Jewish Virtual Library.
halacha_index.summary_he: כפרים נבנים ליד מים. טומאת מת מוסרת במי מנזה ("מי הזאה", העשויים באפר פרה אדומה), בימים השלישי והשביעי, ואחריהם טבילה, ושבעה ימים מחוץ לכפר. גויים נחשבים טמאים.

halacha_index.summary: In Ethiopia women went to the yadam gojo ('hut of blood') for seven days, with a stone boundary and food left outside. They immersed at nightfall with a friend checking. After birth they stayed in the hut until day 8 (son) or 14 (daughter) and were separate for 40 or 80 days.

halacha_index.summary: The fathers arrange the match. Three days of celebration beforehand; the bride dyes her hands and feet red. The kes ties a white-and-red cord (kesherah) from the groom's feet to his forehead. A marriage document 'similar to the standard Jewish Ketuba' is signed by the groom, bride, two witnesses, the kes and a guarantor. Blessing: 'Be fruitful and multiply.' Seven days of celebration, then seven days alone together.
halacha_index.review_notes: In Israel, weddings go through the Rabbinate.
halacha_index.summary_he: האבות מסדרים את השידוך. שלושה ימי חגיגה לפני כן; הכלה צובעת את ידיה ורגליה באדום. הקייס קושר חוט לבן-אדום (קשרה) מרגלי החתן אל מצחו. מסמך נישואין "הדומה לכתובה היהודית הרגילה" נחתם בידי החתן, הכלה, שני עדים, הקייס וערב. הברכה: "פרו ורבו". שבעה ימי חגיגה, ואחר כך שבעה ימים לבדם.

halacha_index.summary: Funerals and the tazkar (commemoration of the dead) gather the community for feasts and prayers led by the kes. Hebrew University booklet fragments indicate a kes on days 3 and 7, a tazkar at the end of the seven days and on the first anniversary (optionally every year), and an animal slaughtered the afternoon before.
